### B267539 — A guard that measures a DURATION fails on healthy code: the pond per-vertex bound sampled each arm once, in the millisecond band where noise lives `[Site Planner / Infra]` (bug) #testing #perf #infra #site-planner  *(minted **B267539** from this branch's reserved block. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `pondViewIndependence`, `superlinear`, `per-vertex`, `offsetInward`, `B227888`, `B236592`, `B221761`, `B221763`, `flaky`, `wall clock`: **B236592/#947** WROTE this test and is not re-opened — its finding (there is no superlinear per-vertex law; the measured exponent is 0.20) is correct and this change does not touch it. The defect is in how the number is SAMPLED. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **Shipped 2026-08-08. Found by it failing the `build` check on PR #957, a branch that does not touch the file, the module under test, or anything either depends on.**
- Verify: sandbox
- **THE FAILURE.** `test/pondViewIndependence.test.js` › *"a single inward offset is not superlinear in vertex count"* went red on CI with `expected 17.674 to be less than 8.464`. Nothing in the branch touches `pondViewIndependence.test.js`, `pondOffset.js` or `pondStageModel.js` — its last change was #947 the previous day.
- **⛔ THE MEASUREMENT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ITEM.** Each arm was timed **once**, over 20 iterations, landing both in the **1–10 ms** band where timer granularity and JIT state dominate. On ONE IDLE MACHINE the single-sample ratio spanned **0.23× … 8.81×** against a **6×** bound — while the TRUE cost ratio, taken as a minimum over repeats, is **1.84×**. The algorithm was never near the bound; the sampling was.
- **AND A SECOND, SUBTLER BUG IN THE SAME LINE: the bound is a function of the baseline.** `max(small, 1) × 6` means a baseline that happens to measure FAST **tightens** the gate. That is backwards — a lucky-fast baseline should never make the test harder to pass — and it is exactly what happened on CI, where `small` came in at 1.41 ms and set the bar at 8.46 ms.
- **THE FIX — the measurement only; the assertion is byte-for-byte unchanged.** Both arms are sampled **repeatedly and INTERLEAVED**, each keeping its **MINIMUM**, at a higher iteration count. Min is the right statistic for *"how fast can this go"*: a scheduler steal, a GC or a noisy neighbour can only ever **add** time, never subtract it, so the minimum is the least-contaminated estimate and one clean sample out of seven suffices. Interleaving stops a machine that drifts mid-run from biasing one arm against the other.
- **⛔ THE CLEANEST PROOF CAME FROM CI ITSELF, AND IT IS BETTER THAN ANY BENCH: THREE CONSECUTIVE RUNS OF A BYTE-IDENTICAL TREE DISAGREED.** PR #957 ran `Build` on `aa8c041f` → **success**, then on `7bbccf67` → **FAILURE**, then on `92cbc26c` → success. **`7bbccf67` is an EMPTY commit on top of `aa8c041f`** (`git diff aa8c041f 7bbccf67` is empty — it was a `--allow-empty` CI nudge). Same tree, same runner image, opposite verdicts, minutes apart. A guard whose answer changes with nothing but the weather is not measuring the code.
- **A/B, MEASURED UNDER THE CONTENTION THAT PRODUCED THE FAILURE (3× CPU load), 40 trials each on healthy code:** old sampling **2/40 false failures**; new sampling **0/40**. Green on six consecutive idle runs and four consecutive loaded runs.
- **⛔ AND A PRE-EXISTING WEAKNESS THIS FOUND, RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY LEFT OR QUIETLY "FIXED".** The 6× bound's SENSITIVITY is weaker than its comment implies. A deliberately planted O(n²) pairwise vertex scan — the shape a self-intersection guard arriving on this path would have — only reaches **~3.4×** at this ring size (**12 vertices against 192**), because at that size `offsetInward` is dominated by fixed clipper overhead. **The bound was NOT changed**: tightening a threshold on the strength of one sandbox, against a CI runner this session cannot measure, would trade a proven flake for an unproven one, and loosening it would be worse. The honest reading is written into the test: this guard proves no quadratic term large enough to change the cost CLASS has arrived — it does not prove none exists. Sharpening it wants a bigger ring or a direct exponent fit, and that is a deliberate follow-on, not a silent edit.
- **THE GENERAL RULE IT RE-CONFIRMS.** `CLAUDE.md` already says this repo has been *"bitten four times in two days by guards that measured how long something took instead of how many times it happened"* — and the sibling test one line above this one says it outright: *"The COUNT of clipper executes, not the time … a machine that happens to be busy cannot [fail here]."* This test could not take that advice, because the question *"is one call superlinear in n?"* has no invocation count to count. **⛔ WHY, and the sentence that decides the design.** The symptom has now failed to reproduce TWICE under instruments we aimed ourselves: the sandbox battery returned an honest null (B1121 §1 — 1,323 → 1,486 ms against a ±6.3% floor, non-monotone), and a live signed-in drive on his own machine found **zero dropped frames in 1,120**, one long task and that one a garbage collection, wall time flat within 0.2%, and no cliff on a 40-step deep zoom into his real PDF overlay. Meanwhile he has reported it consistently for weeks. **When the user hits it and the instrument does not, the instrument is the problem.** So the app records itself, continuously, and keeps the window BEFORE the moment — because by the time anyone reaches for a profiler the episode is over. That is the whole reason for a ring buffer rather than a start button.

**WHAT SHIPPED.**
- **`perfRing.js`** — preallocated ring buffers: ~4,096 interacting frames (time + delta), 192 long animation frames (time, duration, blocking time, interned attribution), 96 counter rows × 11 columns, plus a bounded string table. Fixed-arity pushes, written by index, nothing returned on the hot path.
- **`perfTrigger.js`** — the self-calibrating trigger (below).
- **`perfCapture.js`** — the payload allowlist + the compact encoder.
- **`perfRecorder.js`** — the wiring: an INTERACTION-GATED frame loop, a `long-animation-frame` observer (falling back to `longtask`), a 2 s counter tick that reads the DOM every third tick and skips a hidden tab, and the capture path.
- **`perfRecorderHandle.js`** — the tiny always-loaded half: the kill switch, the bind seam, and the plan/zoom context setters.
- **`perfCaptureStore.js`** — the bounded on-device copy.
- **`perfScene.js`** — `readScene` lifted out of `perfInstrument.js` unchanged, so the always-on recorder can share it without dragging the 25%-sampled instrument into every tab.

**⛔ THE TRIGGER, AND THE NUMBERS, STATED WITH THEIR REASONS (the dispatch asked for exactly this).** His own sentence is the specification — *"if I reload, it's immediately pretty quick and then a minute later or two, it's lagging just to go side to side"* — which describes a machine compared to ITSELF, a minute apart, not to a millisecond constant. So: **the baseline is the MEDIAN frame delta over the window from 5 s to 50 s after load** — skipping the boot, which nobody claims is fast (B1431 attributed four busy seconds there, and folding them in would set a bar nothing could clear) — and firing needs **three** conditions to hold at once over a **two-second** window of frames he is actually interacting through: **(a) LEVEL** — window mean ≥ **2.0×** baseline · **(b) SUSTAIN** — at least **half** the window's frames are individually that slow · **(c) FLOOR** — the window mean is at least **33 ms** in absolute terms.
- **2.0×** because this codebase's own measured run-to-run noise floor is ±6.3% (B1121 §1); a doubling is an order of magnitude clear of it, and it is roughly where a smooth gesture starts to read as a dragging one. Lower trades false alarms for sensitivity there is no budget for — three auto-captures per page load is the whole allowance.
- **two seconds** because it is long enough that no single stall of any cause can fill it and short enough that a bad drag is caught while it is happening.
- **half the frames**, not an average, is what makes it GC-immune: one 400 ms frame in a window of a hundred is one percent, not sixty. This is the dispatch's "not on a single slow frame", enforced rather than intended.
- **33 ms** stops a very fast machine reporting a doubling that is still imperceptible — twice as slow as eight milliseconds is a frame nobody can see. Self-relative alone would fire there.
- **MEDIAN, not mean, for the baseline:** a collection pause during calibration would inflate a mean and quietly raise the bar for the rest of the session — the failure mode where the instrument stops being able to see the problem.
- His display is pinned at **50 Hz**; an absolute threshold tuned to it would be wrong on every other machine, which is the second reason the whole thing is self-relative.

**⚠ A REAL DEFECT IN THAT DESIGN, FOUND BY ITS OWN TESTS AND FIXED BEFORE MERGE — worth recording because the shape recurs.** The sustain window was first qualified by a fixed FRAME COUNT (24 frames in two seconds). That makes the trigger **progressively less able to fire the worse the lag gets**: past about 80 ms a frame there are never 24 of them in a two-second window, so the sessions that most deserve a capture could not produce one at all. The window is qualified by the **TIME it spans** now (≥75% of the sustain period, with a floor of 8 frames): two seconds of evidence is two seconds of evidence whether it is 120 frames or 10. Both ends of the range are asserted — a 4 fps arm and a 144 Hz arm.

**THE MANUAL CONTROL — his perception is the one signal this programme has never had.** A small ◷ button in the planner's existing zoom stack (bottom-right, beside ＋ / － / ⤢), one click away while his hand is already there, deliberately not a menu dive. It captures the seconds BEFORE the press. Manual captures are marked `kind:"manual"` and stay distinguishable from auto-fired ones, because his report is more authoritative than the threshold. It confirms in place and, per LOUD-FAILURE, says so when it recorded nothing rather than looking identical to a success. **Placement is the cheapest thing here to move if he wants it elsewhere.**

**⛔ PRIVACY IS AN ALLOWLIST, NOT A HABIT, AND IT IS PROVED BEFORE EVERY SEND.** The payload is BUILT from `CAPTURE_NUMERIC_KEYS` / `CAPTURE_ENUM_KEYS` and then checked against them by `assertCaptureClean`, which the recorder calls before the row goes out and REFUSES the send on any violation (reporting the refusal). A denylist fails the first time somebody adds a field, which is how telemetry accidents happen. Counters, timings and view state only — no drawing geometry, no parcel or appraisal records, no owner names or addresses, no callout text, no raster bytes. The plan identifier is SANITISED rather than trusted: a plan id here can be a name he typed, so anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` is demoted to a short non-reversible hash (`planIdKind` says which), and attribution strings are stripped of query and path (a URL in this app can carry a plan id). The test drives a deliberately DIRTY fixture — his name, a street address, a callout string, a polygon, a parcel id, raster bytes — and asserts none of it survives anywhere in the encoded row. Same discipline `scripts/extract-plan.mjs` already follows.

**PERSISTENCE — readable with no action from him, and in the RIGHT TIER.** The row travels on the EXISTING `public.client_errors` table via `reportClientEvent("perfcap", …)` — the precedent the dispatch named, and the B468 pattern that needs **no schema migration and no SQL step from him**. That column truncates at 2,000 characters, so the frame track is packed one base-64 character per frame with the rare slow frames carried explicitly (the clamp can never hide a stall) and the encoder **trims oldest-first until it fits, recording what it dropped** — a capture that silently lost its tail would read as a calmer episode than the one that happened. Bounded at ≤ 9 rows per page (3 auto + 6 manual), far under `clientErrors`' shared 100-row per-page ceiling, because a recorder that spends the error channel's budget is a worse regression than any data it collects is worth. The **FULL, untrimmed** capture is kept on the device — **IndexedDB, the LARGE tier, per TIER-BY-REBUILDABILITY**: a diagnostic must never compete with saved plans for the ~5 MB store that was measured 78% full on his machine. Pruned to three on every write, declared `rebuild: NONE / reclaimable: false` (nothing can rebuild a capture — the moment is gone), and **surfaced in the plan menu → Storage with its own Delete control**, so the class can never grow without being visible.

**⛔ GUARD 1 — OVERHEAD, MEASURED, NOT CLAIMED, AND THE FIRST TWO ATTEMPTS AT MEASURING IT WERE WRONG.** `ui-audit/verify-perf-recorder.mjs` (`npm run perf:recorder`, hermetic — no external host, no sign-in, no plan fixture, so it is in CI's reach rather than filed as a live check):
- **TIME: 0.07 µs per frame** against a stated **2.0 µs** bound chosen before the run — 0.0004% of a 16.7 ms frame budget.
- **END TO END: 0 ms** difference in median frame time between recorder ON and OFF, over three interleaved reps of an identical scripted gesture (`?perfrec=off` is both the OFF arm and a real field kill switch; a page with it set never even downloads the recorder chunk).
- **ALLOCATION: guarded STRUCTURALLY, and that decision is a measurement rather than a preference.** Planting a real per-frame object plus a per-frame string in the hot path moved the timing bench from 0.05 to 0.07 µs/frame — nowhere near its bound — because a young-generation bump allocation in a tight loop is about twenty nanoseconds. A heap-delta arm over `performance.memory` was then built **and removed**: without `--enable-precise-memory-info` the value is quantised to 100 KB and cached for twenty minutes (the planted defect read exactly **0** on every run), and with the flag ambient growth only ADDS while a scavenge only SUBTRACTS — so the MAX read **33.6 bytes/frame on a hot path that allocates nothing** and the MIN read **−21.5 on one that allocates ~48**. Both statistics measured, both wrong, and no third rescues a signal that noisy. **A guard that cannot fail on its own defect is decoration**, so it was replaced by a deterministic source rule over the per-frame path (`onFrame` · `pushFrame` · `pushTask` · `pushCounters` · `feedFrame` · `pushWindow` · `evictWindow` · `windowSpan`): no object or array literal, no template literal, no constructor, no spread, no allocating array method, no arrow function. The fire branch was split out of `feedFrame` for exactly this reason — it is the only allocating part and it runs at most three times per page.
- **Bundle cost, paid where it belongs:** the recorder is a **16.6 KB LAZY chunk** fetched in an idle gap after boot (never on any route's critical path — the bundle audit's route closure is over static imports), plus **3.1 KB** on the site route for the control and the handle. `siteRouteChunks` still 7 of 7 and the allowlist clean — the first cut broke both, because a module reachable from a lazy chunk and the site route but NOT the entry gets hoisted into a third chunk that lands on a plain Site load; the handle is imported from `main.jsx` to put it in the entry every route already downloads. `bundle.totalJsBytes` was RATCHETED (4599.1 → 4693.4 KB) with the reason on the record: main was already 73.6 KB above that stale baseline before this branch and 20.6 KB of new lazy code carried it over.

**⛔ GUARD 2 — ANTI-ROT, AND IT IS MUTATION-PROVEN IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.** A recorder that never fires is indistinguishable from a healthy app — the exact failure `count-pond-invocations --assert` and the decode/annotation fault arms exist to close. So the harness **INDUCES a deliberate stall** (a 70 ms-per-frame burn under real driven input) and asserts a capture FIRES: **3 auto-captures**, off a 16.7 ms baseline. A **CONTROL** arm drives the identical gesture with no stall and asserts **0**, so the guard proves the trigger DISCRIMINATES rather than merely that it is loud. **If the stall arm comes back clean the harness exits 1 as NOT OBSERVING** — proven by mutation: raising the perceptibility floor made it report *"NOT OBSERVING: a deliberate stall produced NO capture (baseline 16.7 ms, window mean 77 ms)"* and exit 1. The unit half is mutation-proven too: the planted per-frame object turns the allocation rule red, and renaming a hot-path function turns the NOT-OBSERVING check red rather than leaving it trivially green.

**⛔ THE STOPPING RULE, RECORDED HERE SO IT CANNOT ROT.** **If the recorder sees a week of the owner's normal use and never trips, B1121 closes as FIXED BY #947** — the pond recurrence was measured at **55,760 ms per pan on Quiddity**, which is itself a complete description of *"lagging just to go side to side"*. A week of silence from an instrument that is proven able to fire is evidence, not absence. Conversely, a capture that arrives is the first direct measurement this programme has ever had of the machine that HAS the symptom, and its counters name where to look.

**⚠ AND A HYPOTHESIS, FLAGGED AS A HYPOTHESIS AND NOT A CLAIM.** #947 may already have fixed it: a fresh load starts zoomed out, where ponds may be culled or their labels never fitted, and the work only engages as he zooms and pans into working range — which would present exactly as *"quick after reload, sluggish a minute later"*. **This is a story that fits, nothing more.** This programme has killed five of those, and it is written down only so the next session does not re-derive it and mistake it for a finding. The recorder is what would settle it.

- **⚠ WHAT THE FIXTURE IS AND IS NOT.** The page GEOMETRY is his — 1728 × 2592 pt, ARCH D, one page, 0.55 opacity, 1.5° rotation, both plans. The page CONTENT is synthetic linework (`ui-audit/lib/sheetPdf.mjs`, a real valid PDF, `--strokes` to sweep it), because his drawing does not belong in this repository. The re-raster's cost has two halves — PDF.js's render of the page content, and the PNG encode of the resulting canvas — and only the first is content-dependent, so **this understates the render half and reproduces the encode half exactly.** His real sheet is a full civil drawing; the numbers above are a floor.
- **Shipped:** `ui-audit/zoom-reraster-arms.mjs` (the battery, `npm run perf:reraster`) · `ui-audit/lib/rerasterProbe.mjs` (the pure decision half — it IMPORTS the app's threshold rather than copying it) · `ui-audit/lib/sheetPdf.mjs` (dependency-free PDF generator) · `RERASTER_ARMS` / `rerasterArmFixture` / `pdfStorage` in `ui-audit/lib/planFixture.mjs` · `test/rerasterProbe.test.js` (28, incl. a SOURCE GUARD that the probe's one mirrored piece of app logic has not drifted from `SitePlanner.jsx`).

### B251137 — The fix: a re-raster ladder plus a per-rung cache, so crossing the zoom gate costs one page render instead of one per wheel notch — and zooming back in costs none `[Site Planner]` (bug) #site-planner #perf  *(the fix B251136's measurement produced. Minted **B251137** from the same reserved block. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `re-raster`, `overlayPdf`, `chooseOverlayRasterScale`, `hires`, `B749`, `B1345`, `B1350`, `B1352`, `B1437`, `B1440`: **B749** shipped the path being fixed; **B1345/B1350** are the geometry LOD tier and are a different mechanism (representation change on DRAWN geometry, not raster scheduling); **B1352/B1437/B1440** are the resolve-once/memo boundary, whose IDIOM this follows. Net-new.)*
`[x]` **Shipped 2026-08-08, measured before and after on both of the owner's real Bain plans.**
- Verify: live (zoom-/data-density-dependent rendering + real-project-data — `V48144`, `Blocker: auth`, `Blocker: real-data`)
- **THE CONSTRAINT WAS THE POND CONSTRAINT: do not reduce what is drawn.** PERCEPTUAL-PARITY's relaxation is for detail the owner cannot see at working zoom; a sheet he has deliberately zoomed into is the opposite case. So the bar taken here is not a perceptual measurement but a **PROOF of non-degradation**: `chooseOverlayRasterScale` now rounds the chosen scale **UP** to an octave rung above the base raster, clamped to the 8192 px cap, and both of those steps can only raise it relative to `min(want, cap)` — the exact scale the old continuous rule picked. The returned scale is therefore `>= ` the old one at every zoom and every page size, pinned by a dense sweep in `test/overlayRerasterCount.test.js`. Sometimes it is finer; it is never coarser. **No resolution cap was taken and no detail was dropped** — option (c) from the brief was available and was not needed.
- **What that buys, and why it is a scheduling fix rather than a cheaper algorithm.** With the scale DISCRETE, a zoom sweep asks for the same rung over and over instead of a slightly different scale at every ×1.12 notch, so the answer can simply be kept. On his ARCH-D sheet the whole band between the gate and the cap collapses to **exactly one rung**.
- **And the second half, which is the bigger one: the zoom-out no longer throws the raster away.** The old effect revoked the hi-res the moment the view dropped below the gate — and a zoom sweep is out AND back by definition, so every return trip paid the whole 179 MB page render again. Rungs now live in an LRU cache (`HIRES_CACHE_PER_OVERLAY` = 3 per overlay) that survives a zoom-out; what is retained is the **encoded PNG blob (~3.5 MB)**, never the decoded texture, which the compositor allocates only for the raster actually on screen. Hiding or removing a reference still drops its rungs, and the cache is the only owner of an object URL, so a displayed raster can never be revoked out from under the `<image>` showing it.
- **A third defect the measurement exposed and this closes: a re-raster that arrived while another was in flight was DROPPED AND NEVER RETRIED.** `hiresBusy` made the effect `continue`, with nothing to re-run it, so a fast zoom could leave the overlay on a rung the view had already left until some unrelated dependency changed. A completion now bumps `hiresTick` — **gated on real work having been done**, because an ungated bump is an infinite loop for an overlay whose bytes cannot be fetched.
- **MEASURED, same harness, same regime, both plans.** The `outback` arm (in, back out below the gate, in again — eighteen notches) is the one that shows the cache, and it did not exist before this work because no single-direction sweep can see a revoke-on-zoom-out:

  | arm | re-rasters before → after | main-thread blocked, total, before → after |
  |---|---|---|
  | bain / across | 2 → **1** | 3,347 → **742 ms** (−78%) |
  | bain / outback | 3.5 → **1** | 3,277 → **1,776 ms** (−46%) |
  | quiddity / across | 2 → **1** | 2,046 → **824 ms** (−60%) |
  | quiddity / outback | 4.5 → **1** | 4,842 → **1,563 ms** (−68%) |

  After: **12 of 12 reps at exactly 1**, across both plans and both sweeps, with the controls unchanged and still at zero (`across-image` 0 re-rasters, 94 ms worst block; `below` 0). `--assert` green.
- **⚠ THE COUNT IS THE CLAIM; THE DURATIONS ARE REPORTED WITH THEIR SPREAD.** The re-raster count is deterministic — 12/12 — and it is what the guard asserts. The worst SINGLE main-thread block is not: the same arm on the same build measured 557 ms in the clean 3-rep pass and 1,808 ms in a 2-rep pass an hour earlier. Long-task TOTAL is the stable signal and is what the table reports; a single-block improvement is not claimed beyond "no worse". This is B1434's rule applied to our own result rather than to someone else's.
- **⚠ AND ONE RUN WAS THROWN AWAY, recorded because the failure mode is invisible.** A post-fix pass reported `quiddity/across` at 2 and `quiddity/outback` at 4 — the pre-fix numbers — on the fixed build. `dist` had been rebuilt from a stashed tree WHILE that harness was running, so its early arms measured one build and its later arms measured another. Nothing in the output says so; only the numbers being exactly the pre-fix ones gave it away. **Never rebuild under a running harness**, and prefer a build fingerprint over a memory of which build is on disk (here: the site-route chunk is 2372.2 KB with the fix, 2371.3 KB without).
- **Bundle cost, attributed rather than assumed:** +0.9 KB on the Site route, measured by building the same tree with and without the `src/` change (2372.2 vs 2371.3 KB). The +2.0 KB above baseline and the +74.2 KB on total JS that `perf:bundle` also reports were **already on main** and are not this item's.
- **THE GUARD IS A COUNT, NOT A DURATION, in the idiom B236592/#947 established** — a time budget passes the moment a re-raster that should not happen merely gets cheaper. Two halves, neither substituting for the other: `test/overlayRerasterCount.test.js` (12) replays the production rule AND the pre-fix rule verbatim as a mutation check, so reinstating the revoke-on-zoom-out or the continuous scale goes red; and `node ui-audit/zoom-reraster-arms.mjs --assert` asserts the per-arm budget (`across` 1, `outback` 1, every control 0) against a real browser driving a real wheel gesture, which is the only place the number the app ACTUALLY produces exists.
- **⚠ ONE THING NOT DONE, AND DELIBERATELY.** Option (b) from the brief — raster only the visible REGION rather than the whole page — is the larger win and is NOT taken here. It changes the overlay from one placed image into a viewport-tracked tile, which makes PAN a re-raster trigger where today it is free (VIEW-INDEPENDENT-ONCE), and it would have to be measured against the pan batteries as well as this one. The ladder plus the cache takes the sweep to one page render, which is the number the count guard now holds; region rastering is worth revisiting only if a measurement says one render is still too many.

### B242544 — The Layers panel could not scroll: a percentage max-height resolved to `none`, so the card grew past the map and the list below the fold was unreachable `[Site Planner / UI]` (bug) #site-planner #ui #gis  *(owner report 2026-08-07, verbatim: "obviously horrible, because then I cannot get to everything." Arrived as provisional NEW-1. Minted **B242544** from this branch's reserved block B242544–B242559 against freshly-fetched main d4bcc4a. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `scroll`, `overflow`, `layers panel`, `wheel`, `B1423`, `B1424`, `B484`, `B208966`: **B1423** owns panel-vs-map-chrome z-index and the derived panel height, **B208966** is Review's rail scroll, **B484** is main-thread stalls. No item covers the planner Layers panel refusing to scroll. Net-new — but see the regression provenance below, because this defect was INTRODUCED by B1423.)*
`[x]` **Shipped 2026-08-07 and VERIFIED HERE — headless, on the real render, at four viewport heights, mutation-checked. `Verify: sandbox`.**
- Verify: sandbox — `e2e/layers-panel-scroll-and-state.spec.js` (5 NEW-1 specs), every one proven RED on the pre-fix build
- Origin: filed 2026-08-07 from the owner chat block (NEW-1)

**AUDIT FIRST — the brief named four candidate causes and it was NONE OF THEM.** Each was measured on the real DOM rather than reasoned about, and each was refuted: **(a)** the flexbox `min-height: auto` trap — refuted, every element in the chain already carried `minHeight: 0`; **(b)** an ancestor clipping with `overflow: hidden` — present (the card, for its rounded corners; the map pane) but not the cause, they clip a box that should never have been that tall; **(c)** the scroll container being the wrong element — refuted, the scroll box was written correctly with `flex: 1; minHeight: 0; overflowY: auto`; **(d)** the brief's STRONG CANDIDATE, the wheel-zoom handler eating the gesture — refuted by reading it: `SitePlanner.jsx`'s non-passive wheel listener already opens with `if (e.target.closest("[data-wheelscroll]")) return;` and the Layers card already carries that attribute. **Every module involved was correct in isolation.** The defect existed only in the resolved cascade.

**The actual cause, measured.** The card row between the positioned container and the cards had `maxHeight: "100%"` and therefore a height of `auto`. A percentage `max-height` resolves against the containing block's height **only when that height is definite**; against a content-driven one it computes to `none`. So the Layers card's own `maxHeight: "100%"` silently became no limit at all, the card grew to its full content height, and the scroll box — correctly written — never overflowed and so never scrolled. Measured on a 1280×600 viewport: **the card stood 1568px inside a 500px slot, and the last of 27 rows sat 641px below the bottom of the window.** The fix is one word — `height` instead of `maxHeight` on that row — which makes the percentage resolvable and re-arms every descendant's `maxHeight: "100%"`.
- **It failed at EVERY realistic height, not only short ones** (the brief asked). Because the card resolved to its content height regardless of the room offered, the shortfall scaled with the viewport rather than shrinking: 1000/800/700/600px tall all failed. All four are asserted so a fix that only works with plenty of room cannot pass.
- **It was the panel BODY, not a nested group** (the brief asked). One scroll box, one missing precondition.
- **`pointerEvents` had to move in the same edit, or the fix trades a scroll bug for a dead map.** That row is only as tall as its content today; a full-height version still claiming pointer events would lay an invisible click-eating strip down the right of the map wherever the cards are not — worst with both collapsed. The row is now transparent to the pointer and each card claims its own presses back. Asserted directly: with both cards collapsed, a press 200px below them lands on the canvas.
- **The other side panels do NOT have this bug, and the reason is instructive.** Checked rather than assumed: `FloatingPanel` gets a definite `maxHeight: min(72vh, 620px)` on a `position: fixed` card, and the docked left-rail panels (Properties / Standards / Notes / Yield) sit in a rail whose height is definite from the shell. Both resolve their percentages fine. The shared ancestor that needed fixing had exactly one broken descendant chain, so the fix is in one place — not four, and not a shared abstraction invented for a problem only one surface has.
- **⛔ NO FURNITURE ADDED** (the brief's constraint): no scrollbar chrome, no collapse-all, no virtualization. Three CSS properties on one element, plus the pointer-events consequence.

**⛔ THE PART WORTH REMEMBERING: B1423 INTRODUCED THIS, AND BOTH OF ITS SCROLL GUARDS WENT GREEN ON IT.** B1423 built this flex column and claimed "group headers stick so you can still tell which group you are in after scrolling." Its spec (`e2e/layers-panel-legibility.spec.js`) was re-run against a deliberately re-broken build for this item and **all four specs passed**. Two of them are scroll guards and each rotted green a different way:
- The sticky-header guard proves the list scrolled — but only after **writing the missing precondition in itself**: `scroller.style.maxHeight = "180px"; scroller.style.height = "180px"`. That injected `height` is precisely the definite height the real cascade lacked. **A guard that supplies the precondition whose absence is the bug can never detect it.**
- The "many more than four rows" guard counts rows inside the scroller's rectangle and asserts ≥ 10. On the defect the scroller was 1537px tall, so **all 27 rows were "inside" it** and the check passed emphatically — measuring "rows visible without scrolling" against a box that had grown past the window.
- The new spec avoids both traps by asserting only properties the user can observe: `scrollHeight` vs `clientHeight` on the untouched element, and **a real wheel gesture** rather than `scrollIntoView` (written with `scrollIntoView` the last-row test also passed on the bug — it walks up and scrolls any ancestor that will move, including ones the user cannot reach). The wheel gesture doubles as the standing check on candidate (d).

So a matching Colorado scope is **wells + flowlines** and nothing else — no setback rule, no permit feed, no bottom-hole locations. MATCH SCOPE, DO NOT EXPAND IT.

**The agency name, confirmed:** the Colorado Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (COGCC) was renamed the **Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC)** under SB 23-285. Dataset names, item titles and URLs still say COGCC throughout — the AGOL item that points at the authoritative service is literally named `COGCC_Oil_and_Gas` while its title reads "ECMC Oil and Gas". Do not treat the two names as two sources.

**⛔ WHY NOTHING WAS WIRED — and this is a refusal, not an omission.**
- **The authoritative host is `gisdnr.state.co.us` (Colorado DNR), folder `ECMC_Public`** — e.g. `https://gisdnr.state.co.us/arcgis/rest/services/ECMC_Public/ECMC_Wells/MapServer/0`, published by Colorado's own GIS org (`COLGIS1`). **This is new information B1422 did not have** — it recorded only "ECMC's own host". The endpoint NAME is now on the record; its field names, its sublayer list, whether a FLOWLINES service sits beside the wells one, and its Weld County count are all still unverified.
- **Every route to it is blocked from this sandbox.** `gisdnr.state.co.us`, `ecmc.state.co.us`, `gis.ecmc.state.co.us`, `cogcc.state.co.us`, `gis.colorado.gov`, `data.colorado.gov` and `dwr.state.co.us` all return **HTTP 403 at the egress proxy's CONNECT** (`connect_rejected — gateway answered 403`), i.e. the whole `state.co.us` / `colorado.gov` space. Three public read-relays were tried as an indirect channel and are blocked too. The app's own GIS cache proxy cannot be used either: `ALLOWED_GIS_HOST_RE` in `gisProxyCore.js` carries no Colorado host, and widening an open-proxy allow-list purely to probe an endpoint would be shipping unverified config to production.
- **The county-clip trap is REAL and was re-confirmed independently.** Searching AGOL for a reachable substitute returns exactly the three services B1422 caught: Adams County's `COGCC_Oil_and_Gas` (explicitly "clipped to the Adams County boundary"), Broomfield's, and a 2022 snapshot from an advocacy org. Wiring any of them into a **Weld County** site is the Chambers-County 14-vs-8,014 failure verbatim.
- **So the standard is B1105's:** the endpoint is named, the math/plumbing already exists, and the DATA is left unwritten rather than guessed. `test/gisRegistryHealth.test.js` already fails if anyone adds a clipped row.

**WHY THIS IS NOT COSMETIC, verified (the brief asked).** The owner's Colorado site is in **Weld County**, which sits over the **DJ Basin / Wattenberg Field** and is the most heavily drilled county in the state — tens of thousands of wells. In **April 2017 a home in Firestone, Weld County exploded**, killing two people; the cause was traced to a **severed, abandoned flowline** from a nearby well that had been left uncapped and was leaking gas into the soil. Colorado's flowline registration, integrity-testing and mapping rulemaking followed directly from it. That is exactly why a Weld developer needs flowlines located before design — and exactly why an EMPTY oil & gas layer there is **dangerous rather than merely unhelpful**: on a due-diligence screen a blank reads as all-clear. Which is the whole reason the B1422 ×2 work below refuses to hide the row.

**To unblock:** allow `gisdnr.state.co.us` outbound (or add it to the GIS proxy allow-list after a manual verification), then probe `ECMC_Public` for the wells + flowlines sublayers, take statewide and Weld-point counts the way all 41 Colorado fixtures were taken, and add the rows with `states: ["CO"]`. Per the registry architecture this should be **registry rows only** — the panel, the demotion, the merge handling and the state gate are all general and already carry Colorado.

### B233152 — The double-click audit certified a pond NOBODY COULD CLICK: three independent holes, each of which alone makes the suite green over a dead feature `[Site Planner / Infra]` (bug) #site-planner #testing #infra #selection  *(filed 2026-08-07 from the owner's live V17005 report — "your harness certifies an element type that is broken on real data". Minted **B233152** from this branch's reserved block B233152–B233167 against freshly-fetched main c55ce52. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open / ⏳ Verify / Done across `double-click`, `dblclick`, `audit-doubleclick`, `pond click`, `selection`, B50008–B50011, B1174, B1327, B922, B261: **B50011** owns the harness itself and this is its first real defect report, filed separately rather than as a recurrence because the harness's own blind spots are a distinct fault from the click contract it tests. Net-new.)*

**The report.** V17005 passed live on both features the owner double-clicked, and the same pass found a DETENTION POND on the Bain plan dead to a double-click AND to a single click — while `ui-audit/audit-doubleclick-properties.mjs` seeded a pond and passed it 19/19 in all three modes.

**AUDIT-FIRST — three holes, found by attacking the harness rather than the pond. Each is independently sufficient to green a dead element, which is why the fixture-data theory alone was never going to explain it.**

1. **AN UNANSWERED PROBE POINT WAS PRESSED ANYWAY.** `probePoint` falls back to its first candidate when NO point resolves to the feature. The loop then clicked it, the press landed on whatever lay beneath, *some* panel opened, and `panelOpen()` — which only ever asked "is a panel up", never "is it THIS feature's panel" — reported a pass. **Measured, not argued: with the pond's own group forced to `pointer-events: none` — a pond provably unclickable — the suite still reported 50/50.** An unanswered probe is now a FAILURE with its own message: if nothing under a feature claims it, the user cannot reach it either, and that IS the bug being hunted.
2. **SELECTION WAS NEVER ASSERTED AT ALL.** The owner's symptom was "no panel, **no selection**", and the suite had no check for the second half — a feature that silently refuses selection was indistinguishable from one that selects fine. Now every feature must select on a single click, in every mode (locked is select-only per B922; grouped selects its group per B261, so "something is selected" is the common floor). The deselect is a PRECONDITION, not politeness: Escape alone was measured leaving 45 handle nodes up, and without proving zero first the assertion would pass for every feature whether or not the press did anything.
3. **A CENTRES-MODE PROBE COULD LAND ON TEXT.** `pointer-events` is inherited but a CHILD may override it, so a pointer-dead pond still had live chrome: its map label. The probe found the label, NEW-3 forwarded the press from text to the body's action, and the row passed over a body nobody can press. Centres mode now requires a GEOMETRY hit (text / tspan / `[data-el-dim]` / `[data-label-for]` rejected) — `--labels`, whose entire purpose is probing the label, is the deliberate exception. Interior off-centre candidates were added in the same change, because a filled feature carries its label AT its centre and rejecting text without them would report a perfectly clickable pond as unreachable.

**Two source changes, both inert, both required — selection had no DOM signal to read.** An element (unlike a markup) carries no per-feature "selected" stamp, and a multi/group selection paints only chrome that renders OUTSIDE the handle layer. `SelectionChrome.jsx` and the multi-selection footprint ring now stamp `data-testid="selection-chrome"` / `data-testid="selection-ring"`. One attribute each on already pointer-transparent groups; no visual change. **Bundle cost: +0.2 KB on `bundle.siteRouteJsBytes` (2369.3 → 2369.6 KB), inside the headroom band and stated rather than absorbed silently.** It stays: the two attributes ARE the fix for an unobservable selection, and there is no cheaper way to make selection readable from the DOM than naming the node that paints it.

**Fixture gap closed too — a type name in a fixture is not a class.** The pond row was a bare rect with a label. A real pond carries a detention record, is often an irregular POLYGON (a different branch of `renderElPx` entirely), and may carry an expansion BASELINE painting a second fill over the basin. Added: polygon · rect+detention · polygon+detention · polygon+expansion-baseline · a GROUPED pair. The grouped rows assert **B261 drill-in** in the direction it actually holds (selects, Properties deliberately stays shut), so the one element class whose double-click is *supposed* not to open the panel is PINNED rather than left looking like a pass.

**Verification.** 50/50 `centres` · 50/50 `--labels` · 48/48 `--locked` on merged main. **Negative control, proven RED first:** with the pond group `pointer-events: none`, the pre-fix suite reported **50/50** and the post-fix suite fails **all 12 pond rows** naming the reason. One reported gap is logged, never silently skipped (CLAUDE.md "no silent caps"): a **locked + grouped** element paints no DOM-observable selection at all — locked suppresses handles, grouped paints no per-feature stamp — so `sel` moves with no observable consequence. Reported rather than asserted, because asserting either direction would pin behaviour nobody has decided on.

**Verify: sandbox** — the harness is the deliverable and its own negative control proves it.

Nothing was removed from the picture; 54 vertices were.**

- **THE RESULT — 4 arms × 6 reps interleaved, 24 runs, 0 suppressed** (medians per pan gesture):

  | arm | work ms | vs baseline | render ms | canvas nodes |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | `quiddity` (SLOW) | 55,760 | — | 9,330 | 752 |
  | `one-pond` | 39,505 | −29.2% ✅ 6/6 p=0.031 | 10,017 | 742 |
  | **`simple-ponds`** | **5,955** | **−89.3%** ✅ 6/6 p=0.031 | **3,328** ✅ 6/6 | **752** |
  | `original` (FAST) | 4,940 | −91.1% ✅ 6/6 p=0.031 | 2,806 | 598 |

- **⛔ SO B227477's FINDING 3 IS RE-READ, and that correction is the point of this item.** `one-pond` removed a pond AND its 20 vertices; this arm shows the **vertices** were what it was buying. Pond COUNT is not the cost — both plans draw ponds. It is not "a pond is worth 400 elements", it is **"a vertex is expensive, and ponds are where the vertices are."**
- **THE SCALE, since 54 removed vertices bought 49,806 ms: roughly 920 ms per vertex.** No per-element or per-node model produces that figure, and it points at something **superlinear in ring vertex count** rather than a fixed per-pond cost. Landing zone: `labelFitLadder`'s `interiorFitter` (rasterises the ring, enumerates maximal inscribed rectangles — **B221761**) and the pond ledger rebuilt in the render body (**B221763**). Both are open items that already own pond cost; this says they are worth far more than either estimated.
- **REPLICATION, which is worth as much as the new arm.** This battery ran with **no basemap tiles** (so its render column and its layer count are NOT comparable to B227477's), but the two shared arms reproduced on work at **55,760 vs 55,876** and **4,940 vs 5,157** — the headline result independently reproduced to within a few per cent under a different tile regime. Render separates here too (−64.3%, 6/6) because no rep was contaminated and the floor came out ±13.2% rather than ±116.3%.
- **NEXT, and it is not another fixture subtraction:** *which* per-vertex path is superlinear. That wants the recompute probe (VIEW-INDEPENDENT-ONCE) pointed at a real 48-point ring, not another arm.
- **⛔ ANSWERED BY B236592 (2026-08-07), AND THE ANSWER CORRECTS THIS ITEM'S HEADLINE — "a vertex is expensive" is wrong in the same way B227477's Finding 3 was.** No per-vertex path is superlinear; nothing on this path is superlinear in vertex count at all, and `interiorFitter` costs **0.5 ms of the 55,760 ms gesture**. **Collinear midpoint insertion** — which raises vertex count while holding area, perimeter, bounding box and the drawn path EXACTLY, and so has zero confounds where decimation has one — measures an exponent of **0.20** (16× the vertices, 1.75× the cost). Decimation preserved the *bounding box*, but a bounding box is not a shape: it also removed the **concavity** that loads clipper's intersection sweep, so this arm was still measuring two variables. The real cause was **156 recomputations of the whole stage-storage model per pond per pan** (`drainFacts()` gates rather than memoises), and the "920 ms per vertex" figure was `49,806 ÷ 54` — a recurrence divided by whichever variable the arm named. Fixed under B236592: **55,760 → 505 ms with the real rings untouched.** This block is kept verbatim because a measurement is a historical fact about what was run.
- **⛔ THE BOUNDING-BOX PROPERTY IS WHAT MAKES THIS A ONE-VARIABLE ARM, and it is asserted in the test rather than assumed.** Plain index sampling would shrink each ring, and a ring that shrinks has also changed its painted area, its label-fit question and its overlap with every neighbouring element — three fresh confounds traded for one removed. `decimateRing` pins the four extreme vertices (min-x / max-x / min-y / max-y) first and fills the rest with evenly-spaced indices, so the output is a coarser polygon of **the same extent, in the same place, in the same winding order**. Deterministic, so reps are comparable.
- **WHAT EACH OUTCOME WOULD MEAN.** Simplified rings recover the time ⇒ the cost is ring COMPLEXITY, it lands on the `interiorFitter` / pond-ledger path B221761 and B221763 already own, and the fix is engineering — a cheaper fit, or a coarser ring for the fit question only — with **nothing asked of the owner**. They do not ⇒ the cost is per-POND, and the question becomes what a pond does on every frame that a building does not.
- **⛔ NEITHER OUTCOME LICENSES "DRAW FEWER OR SIMPLER PONDS."** Those are his detention basins; their shape IS the design, and it is surveyed. A separating arm names a cost to go make cheaper — the same bar §2.2's rotation arm is held to. This line is on the item, not only in the doc, because it is the one way this result could be misread into a product instruction.
- **Tests.** `test/planFixture.test.js` 42 (was 39) — the arm's one-variable property, the exact bounding-box preservation, and `decimateRing`'s determinism / ordering / no-op cases. Recorded in `docs/PERF-REAL-PLANS.md` §5.5.

- **⛔ FINDING 1 — the observation is REAL, and the natural experiment is the strongest arm in the set because nothing was synthesised in it.** Two plans of the same site, same overlay, same underlay, same settings; one is eleven times the other. - **⛔ FINDING 2 — THE EASEMENT HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED, ON BOTH HALVES, AND I AM REPORTING IT AS LOUDLY AS THE FINDING because the brief demanded exactly that.** This was the mechanism the asymmetry census made most plausible: 3 pipeline easements vs 0, 50 points of banded geometry, and a constraint relation that scales with easements × elements. `no-easements` removes the geometry AND the relation: **+1.3%, cheaper in 1 of 6 reps, p = 0.219.** `unrestricting` removes only the relation: **+1.4%, 2 of 6, p = 0.688.** **Neither DRAWING an easement nor EVALUATING it costs anything measurable here.** The discriminating arm (d) was designed before any number existed and it discriminated — it just returned the answer that both halves are null. That is a real result, not a failed measurement.
- **⛔ FINDING 3 — the PONDS are implicated, and the size of it is the point.** Removing ONE pond — one element out of fifty-two — takes 15,337 ms off every pan: **−27.4%, cheaper in 6 of 6 paired reps, p = 0.031.** Against B1435's measured 38.5 ms/element that single element is worth **≈ 400 elements**. But the arm removed a pond **and its 20 vertices at once**, so it cannot yet separate pond COUNT from ring COMPLEXITY. **⛔ RE-READ BY B227888, which ran that arm: it is the VERTICES. Coarsening both rings while HOLDING pond count at two recovers 89.3% of a 91.1% gap — so this finding is right about where the cost lives and wrong about what it scales with, and the correct statement is "a vertex is expensive, and ponds are where the vertices are."** Kept as measured rather than rewritten.
- **⛔ FINDING 4 — `render` separates on the pair and on NOTHING else, and the reason is a known defect in the estimator, not a null.** The range-based noise floor came out **±116.3% on render** — set by a single contaminated `quiddity` rep at 22,459 ms against a ~10,500 median. A range floor is monotonically increasing in n, so one bad rep raises the bar above every real effect; this is why every arm's render row reads INCONCLUSIVE while the paired sign test on the same numbers reads 6/6. **Read the paired test, not the floor.** (`work`'s floor was a healthy ±4.6%.)
- **What this does NOT license.** No fix is implied yet. "Two ponds is slow" is not a finding a user can act on — and **B227888 has since shown it is not even true**: the cost is ring vertex count, and it is an engineering cost to go make cheaper, with nothing asked of the owner about how he draws his basins.
- **THE FOUR ARMS, one variable each** (`ui-audit/annotation-arms.mjs --plan bain-pair`): **(a)** `original` vs `quiddity`, both unmodified — the natural experiment, no synthetic change anywhere; **(b)** `no-easements` — the 3 pipeline easements removed; **(c)** `one-pond` — the second pond removed, easements kept; **(d)** `unrestricting` — easements DRAWN but `restrictsBuildings`/`restrictsPaving` forced false.
- **⛔ (d) IS THE ARM THAT CAN DISCRIMINATE, and it was designed before any number existed.** An easement is two things at once: a banded polygon that is DRAWN, and a constraint EVALUATED against every building and paving element. (b) removes both and cannot tell them apart; (d) removes only the second. **If (d) separates while (b) does not, the cost is the constraint RELATION** — which scales with easements × elements, not with easements — and simplifying the drawn band would buy nothing.
- **⛔ THE GUARD IS STRONGER HERE THAN ON SYLVESTRI, and it had to be.** Both Bain plans composite a real 1728×2592 overlay, and IndexedDB is origin-scoped — so the bain-pair path does the two-navigation seed the raster battery uses, and then PROVES the overlay reached the canvas. Skipping that would not merely produce a false null: it would destroy the experiment, because the entire force of this pair is that the overlay is IDENTICAL in both halves, and an absent raster is identical in neither.
- **Instrument note.** `annotation-arms.mjs` grew a `--plan` selector (`sylvestri` | `bain-pair`); the Sylvestri arms, their result and their guard are untouched.

Read only the site row and a 47-element plan reports as **zero elements** — which is precisely how a plan can look empty and unmeasurable.
- **ACCEPTANCE — every value the owner supplied was checked against the database and every one MATCHED.** Bain (`smr9olizi5ue`, "Concept - Original", fortbend): 47 els + 5 parcels · building 11, sidewalk 10, parking 10, road 8 (34 pts), paving 5, trailer 2, pond 1 · 38 of 47 rotated · 0/0/0 markups/measures/callouts · overlay 1728×2592 @ 0.55, `ftPerPx` 2.7777777777777777, page 1, locked, fromIdb, **rotation 1.5** · underlay 1800×1167, fromMap, opacity 1. Sylvestri (`sms4zs8unbkg`, "Concept D - Sylvestri Retail", harris): 98 els + 3 parcels · building 31, parking 23, sidewalk 18, paving 14, road 7 (33 pts), trailer 5 · 73 of 98 rotated · 16 callouts, 4 markup polygons, 2 markup easements, 2 measures · **NO sheet overlay** · underlay 1800×1656, fromMap.
- **⛔ WHY THE OLD FIXTURE IS DELETED RATHER THAN KEPT.** It was guarded by a byte-identity check against its own generator, and **that check was green for the fixture's entire life — while its coordinates were invented.** That is the exact limit of a regeneration guard: it proves a file matches the thing that produced it and says nothing about whether that thing was making the plan up. A synthesised fixture left in the tree is one somebody measures again by accident. The replacement guard is `test/realPlanFixtures.test.js`, which asserts each file against the owner's MEASURED CENSUS — strictly stronger, because it also catches a fixture that regenerates cleanly from a dump that was itself wrong.
- **TWO FACTS THE SYNTHESIS DID NOT HAVE, and both are load-bearing.** (a) The sheet overlay is **rotated 1.5°** — the synthesis said 0, so every arm ever run in this program composited it axis-aligned (B227473 is the arm). (b) The underlay is `fromMap` carrying a **live ArcGIS `World_Imagery/export` URL and NO `idbKey`** — it is FETCHED, not read out of IndexedDB, which corrects `docs/PERF-BAIN.md` §8. `dropIdbBackedSrc` strips the src of anything idb-backed, so a raster that KEPT its src is proof it never was one. §7 (it is never *painted*) is unaffected and stands.
- **REDACTION, and the one place the existing redactor was doing the wrong thing.** `scripts/plan-dump-to-fixture.mjs` is the boundary: the dump is an INPUT that must never be committed, what comes out of it is safe. New in `redactPlan`: **county appraisal records are stripped by name** (`attrs`/`acct`/`addr` — measured at 5.2 KB across Bain's 5 parcels and 3.1 KB across Sylvestri's 3, carrying `OWNER_NAME`, `MAIL_ADDR`, `LAND_VALUE`, `owner_name_1`; nothing in any render path reads them). And callout text is now a **SHAPE-PRESERVING stand-in** rather than `"Note 3"`: exact line count, exact per-line length, whitespace positions VERBATIM (so every word-wrap break lands where it really does), case and character class by representative. The old behaviour destroyed the very property the fixture exists to reproduce — a callout's cost IS its text — and would have made B227474's annotations-present arm understate its own effect. ⚠ Per-glyph advance width is NOT preserved and the doc says so.
- **`sylvestri-concept-d.json` IS NOT TOUCHED AND IS NOT THE SAME ARTEFACT.** It is a 22-element geometry bag pulled 2026-07-31 for `test/zoneAlongAnchor.test.js` + `e2e/dock-zone-anchor.spec.js`, and **three of the ids it drives (`e1454698mwpaoj`, `e1454699mwpaoj`, `e1454796yyuqqs`) have since been DELETED from the live plan.** Overwriting it with the full plan would have taken those tests' hosts away without failing anything at pull time. The new file is `sylvestri-concept-d-full.json`; a test asserts both facts so the two can never be conflated.
- **Consumers repointed:** `raster-arms.mjs`, `boot-tail.mjs` (which also gains `--fixture sylvestri`), `test/planFixture.test.js`, `ui-audit/README.md`, `docs/PERF-BAIN.md`.
- **Tests.** `test/realPlanFixtures.test.js` (30 new) — the acceptance census for both plans, a leak negative (no uuid, no Storage key, no data URL, no appraisal record), the shape-preserving-text properties, and the blank-canvas schema guards (a road without `rot`, or a `vtx` radius with no `treatment`, resolves the whole VIEW to NaN and renders zero elements without throwing — a fixture in that state measures as "this plan is fast") now running over BOTH plans. `test/planFixture.test.js` 32 green.

### B227473 — The overlay's 1.5° rotation costs about half of what having the overlay at all costs `[Site Planner / Infra]` (task) #site-planner #perf #infra #testing  *(filed 2026-08-07 from the owner chat block as NEW-2, verbatim: "A rotated raster cannot take an axis-aligned fast path … Report the result even if it is null: this program has already mis-reported nulls that were measured on scenes structurally incapable of containing the effect, and a refutation here is worth as much as a finding." Minted **B227473 / V24896** from the same reserved block as B227472. DEDUPE-FIRST — searched Open + ⏳ Verify + Done across `rotation`, `rotate`, `raster`, `overlay`, `blit`, `resample`, `arm`, `B209568`, `B749`, `B73`, `B1433`: **B209568** built the six-arm battery and its `opaque`/`quarter`/`no-overlay` arms are untouched and still stand — this is a SEVENTH arm on a term none of them varied, and it could not have existed before B227472 because the fixture said `rotation: 0`, so an arm forcing it to 0 would have been the baseline wearing a different name and would have reported a guaranteed null. **B749** owns the PDF zoom re-raster, which fires on zoom and is still unmeasured. Net-new.)*
`[ ]` **MEASURED, AND IT SEPARATES. Taking the rotation to 0 is CHEAPER in 6 of 6 paired reps (sign test p = 0.031), median −10.2% render / −12.6% raster — the second-largest raster effect this program has found, behind only removing the overlay outright.**
- Verify: live · `Blocker: real-data` — every figure here is a lower bound with the network absent; the owner's own machine and his own overlay bytes are V24896.
- Origin: filed 2026-08-07 from chat
- **THE ARM.** `unrotated` takes the sheet overlay's rotation 1.5° → 0 and holds **pixel count, `ftPerPx`, opacity, position, `page`, `locked`, `encodedBytes` and the on-map footprint EXACTLY** — unit-tested, the same invariant `quarter` holds for size and for the same reason: an arm that changed two things isolates nothing. The underlay is deliberately untouched (it was never rotated, so touching it would confound).
- **WHY IT IS A PLAUSIBLE MECHANISM AND NOT A FISHING TRIP.** `renderSheetOverlay` wraps the `<image>` in `rotate(θ cx cy)`. An axis-aligned blit — one source pixel copied to one destination pixel — is not available under a rotation; every destination pixel must be resampled from a neighbourhood. B209568's finding 2 established that the overlay's cost tracks **the screen AREA it covers** rather than its resolution, and rotation is the one remaining term that changes how that area is produced.
- **⚠ WHAT THE ARM CANNOT HOLD, stated rather than glossed.** Rotating a rectangle enlarges its axis-aligned BOUNDING BOX, so the rotated arm covers slightly more screen area. That is not a confound to be corrected away — it is inherent to the change under test, and given finding 2 it is a candidate MECHANISM. A separating result reads as "rotation costs something", **never yet as "resampling costs something"**; distinguishing the two needs a third arm and is not claimed.
- **THE RESULT.** 3 arms × 6 reps, interleaved, 18 runs, 0 suppressed. Render total `bain` **2526 ms** → `unrotated` **2255 ms**; raster **2117 → 1851 ms (−12.6%)**, which is where essentially all of it lives — paint, composite and layerize each move ~1% or less, and main-thread work does not separate at all (2/6, p = 0.688), the same blindness B209568's finding (e) describes. It clears the unpaired range floor too (−10.7% against ±8%).
- **PUT NEXT TO THE ARMS THAT CAME BEFORE IT, this is the second-largest raster effect found.** Removing the overlay entirely −24.3% raster · **its 1.5° rotation −12.6%** · three quarters of its pixels −6.3% · its alpha, not separated. **A 1.5° rotation costs about half of what having the overlay at all costs, and about twice what quartering its texture does.** Coherent with B209568's finding (b) rather than in tension with it: the cost is in rasterising the screen AREA the overlay occupies, and rotation is the term that changes how expensively each destination pixel is produced.
- **⛔ WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED.** The arm changes rotation, and rotation changes two things at once — resampling cost per destination pixel AND the size of the axis-aligned bounding box. This says rotation costs something. It does NOT say resampling does. Separating them needs a further arm (an unrotated overlay grown to the rotated bounding box) and nobody has run one.
- **⚠ AND THIS IS NOT THE OWNER'S WHOLE ROTATION STORY.** 1.5° is what his OVERLAY carries. **38 of his 47 Bain elements and 73 of his 98 Sylvestri elements are also rotated** — a term no arm in this program has ever varied either, on a tier this one does not touch.
- **`decodeFault` stays armed**, per the owner's instruction: an arm whose raster never decoded looks exactly like an arm that is fast. Zero reps suppressed across both batteries.

`[ ]` **MEASURED. Removing all 24 annotations is CHEAPER in 6 of 6 paired reps (sign test p = 0.031), median −12.6% of render work — the first non-null result on this axis in the program. No single KIND separates on its own, and that is a result, not a shortfall.**

- Origin: filed 2026-08-07 from chat
- **THE MISS, and it is the same shape as the raster one.** Every plan this program has measured reads **0 / 0 / 0 / 0** on markups, measures, callouts and cross-sections. Goose Creek does; Bain does. So every null result about annotation cost was structurally guaranteed before the first gesture — the admission `docs/PERF-BAIN.md` §0 makes about rasters, on the other tier.
- **WHY SYLVESTRI IS A CLEAN CONTROL and not merely the available plan.** It has **NO SHEET OVERLAY AT ALL.** Nothing it shows can be charged to a raster, to blending, or to texture memory — the three hypotheses the sixty-run Bain battery was about. Its only raster is the `fromMap` underlay the app never paints on a plan with an origin.
- **(a) THE TIER SEPARATES.** `no-annotations` vs baseline: **6/6 paired reps cheaper, p = 0.031, median −12.6%** render, and it also clears the unpaired range floor (−13.8% against ±8.9%). 5 arms × 6 reps, 30 runs, 0 suppressed, interleaved.
- **(b) NO SINGLE KIND SEPARATES, AND THAT IS A RESULT.** Callouts 5/6 (p = 0.219) · markups 5/6 (p = 0.219) · measures 2/6 (p = 0.688). The whole tier clears the bar and none of its parts does — consistent with the cost being DISTRIBUTED across callouts and markups at roughly half the tier's magnitude each, below what six paired reps can resolve individually, with measures contributing nothing. Six reps is the arithmetic minimum at which a sign test can reach p ≤ 0.05 at all (6/6 → 0.031). ⛔ **Do not read this as "callouts are free."**
- **(c) `no-measures` CAME BACK DEARER (+3.2%), which is how you know the floor is honest.** Two measurements cannot cost negative work. That arm has one rep at 2372 ms against a 1300 ms median — visible because every rep is printed — and the verdict correctly reports INCONCLUSIVE rather than a finding in either direction.
- **(d) MAIN-THREAD WORK DOES NOT SEPARATE HERE EITHER** — −8.1%, inside the ±16.6% floor, 5/6 (p = 0.219). The same pattern as `PERF-BAIN.md` §5: the difference lives in paint and raster, and `Script + Layout + RecalcStyle` is blind to both.
- **(e) THE NODE CENSUS, which needs no statistics.** The 24 annotations are **159 canvas nodes and 33 text nodes**: callouts 122 nodes / 30 text · markups 27 / 3 · measures 10 / 0. Callouts are ~77% of the tier's DOM by node count.
- **⛔ THE GUARD, and it earned its keep on the first run.** An arm whose annotations never rendered looks exactly like an arm that is fast — the `decodeFault` principle on a new axis. `annotationFault` proves each arm's callouts, markups and measures reached the canvas, counted from the DOM, before it will report a number. On run one every arm read **0 of 24 annotations on a page rendering all of them**: the census read was written as a template-literal string, and **Playwright evaluates a string as an EXPRESSION and does not call it with the argument, unlike Puppeteer** — the same subtlety that wrote nothing to IndexedDB in B209568, arriving by a different door. Nothing but the guard would have caught it.
- **ONE APP CHANGE, inert.** Markups were the only drawn object with **no id in the DOM at all** (elements have `data-el-id`, measurements `data-measure`, callouts `data-testid="callout-<id>"`), so nothing outside React could tell whether one had rendered. All ten of `renderMarkupNode`'s return paths now carry `data-markup={m.id}` — an attribute with no behaviour attached. A kind that quietly did not carry it would read as "this markup costs nothing".

- **THE QUESTION, as B209568 left it.** *"304 layers against 118 is the largest deterministic difference between the two plans, it is identical across every raster arm, and nothing in this dispatch explains where it comes from."* Two data points support several readings, and the obvious one is that layer count tracks how much is in the scene.
- **WHAT THE REAL PLANS ADD.** Sylvestri is a **third data point from a real plan with 98 elements — roughly twice Bain's — and no raster overlay at all.** That is the observation that discriminates between "layers track scene size" and every other reading, and it is only available because B227472 landed a plan nobody could open.

Bain has the FEWEST elements of the three and the MOST layers; Sylvestri has **more than twice Bain's element count and 118 FEWER layers.** Stripping 159 canvas nodes out of Sylvestri moves the layer count by zero; hiding BOTH of Bain's rasters moves it by zero.
- **(b) WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS: the number of basemap tiles Leaflet holds in the DOM, plus four fixed layers.** Exact on every plan, in every arm, in every run, across two independent harnesses. That one identity explains everything B209568 recorded about this number and could not account for — why it was identical across all six raster arms (no raster arm touches the basemap), why it is identical across all five annotation arms, and why "304 against 118" read as the largest deterministic difference between two plans when it is a difference between two CAMERAS.
- **(c) ⛔ SO ONE CLAUSE OF B209568's FINDING (d) IS WITHDRAWN.** It reads *"roughly half is Bain's own scene: 1,035 canvas nodes against 884, and 304 compositor layers against 118."* The node count stands as a scene difference. **The layer count does not belong in that sentence** — it is a basemap-retention difference that would be there with an empty plan. The composite (+55.6%) and layerize (+46.4%) gaps it was offered as an explanation for are real, are unaffected, and are once again UNEXPLAINED.
- **(d) AND THE NUMBER ITSELF WAS MEASURED ON THE WRONG PLAN.** The real Bain reads **320 layers / 598 canvas nodes**, not 304 / 1,035 — the synthesised fixture was a larger, differently-shaped scene. 320 is the figure to quote, and the reason to quote it is that it is 316 tiles, not a plan.
- **WHAT THIS LEAVES OPEN, stated so it is not mistaken for closed.** *Why* Bain's camera retains 316 tiles where Goose Creek's retains 114. That is a tile-budget / overscan question about the initial fit and the retention policy (`lib/tileBudget.js`, `lib/tileLifecycle.js`), NOT a scene-complexity question — and it is the well-posed version of what §7.3 was asking for. Whether 316 retained tiles is itself a COST is a separate measurement nobody has taken.
- **Recorded in `docs/PERF-REAL-PLANS.md` §3**, with a correction banner at the top of `docs/PERF-BAIN.md`. ⚠ The old report's numbers are kept VERBATIM rather than restated against the real plan: a measurement is a historical fact about what was run, and quietly editing one is how a report stops being evidence.

- **THE DEFECT.** `interiorFitter(ring).spots(w, h, want)` rasterises a pond's polygon at 96 cells across its long axis and enumerates every maximal inscribed rectangle — thousands. The RASTER was cached per ring (a WeakMap); **the SCAN over those rectangles was not**, and `layoutLabels` runs in the render body, so it re-ran up to nine times per pond per frame. **And none of it depends on the pan:** `spots` is asked in FEET (`layoutLabels` divides the screen size by `ppf` first) and a pan is a pure translation at constant scale (B1440), so the ring, the ppf, the lines and the type metrics are bit-for-bit identical frame to frame. Every frame re-asked an identical question and got an identical answer; only the screen ORIGIN moved, and the caller applies that with one multiply-add afterwards.
- **THE FIX, and it is BYTE-IDENTICAL BY CONSTRUCTION** — same pure function, same arguments, same outputs, moved from *once per frame* to *once per distinct question*. No threshold, no approximation, no level-of-detail decision, so **PERCEPTUAL-PARITY has nothing to measure and no pixel argument is made**: byte-identical is the stronger claim and it is the true one. (1) `spots` is memoised on a bounded LRU inside the fitter, whose lifetime IS the ring's — `fitterCache` is a WeakMap keyed on the ring array, so an edited pond arrives as a NEW array and gets a new fitter. **It can never serve a stale interior**, which is the failure that would matter: a label placed against the wrong interior is a wrong drawing, and a wrong drawing is worse than a slow one. (2) An early-out: no rectangle can exceed `maxW`/`maxH`, so a request past either bound was already guaranteed to scan everything and return nothing — turning the WORST case (a label that fits nowhere, exactly the case the outside rung exists for) from a full scan into a comparison.
- **PROVEN ON THE SAME PROBE.** Seeded pond ladder, same regime: per-pond **10.26 → 4.94 ms** of main-thread work per gesture; the 16-pond penalty **+30.5% → +14.1%**. Re-profiled, the phase it was aimed at moves as predicted: Label layout & collision across 0 → 16 ponds **+76.7 ms → +20.0 ms (−74%)**, and `labelFitLadder` is no longer the hottest application function.
- **Bundle.** `perf-bundle-audit` green. This change costs **0.3 KB** on every metric, measured by building with and without it. `bundle.largestChunkBytes` reads **+28.4 KB above its baseline with only 3.6 KB of band left** — that drift was **already on `main` before this branch** (+28.1 KB with this change stashed) and is tracked by **B1064**; it is reported here rather than absorbed, because the next change to touch this chunk has almost no room. No ceiling raised, no baseline re-recorded (**B1178** remains open).
- **Tests.** `test/labelFitMemo.test.js` (8), **mutation-checked two ways** — dropping `want` from the cache key goes red, an off-by-one early-out goes red. The headline test drives a hostile ring battery (square · hourglass · L · sliver) **plus the owner's own Goose Creek pair and two of the four Bain / Concept A basins** through several hundred size questions and asserts the memoised answer is position-for-position, order-for-order, count-for-count what a fresh un-memoised fitter returns; plus an end-to-end check that a PANNED frame places the label at exactly the panned offset, on the same rung, saying the same words. `labelFitLadder` / `pondLabelFit` / `geometryLod` unchanged and green. Lint clean · `npm test` green · build green · `perf-bundle-audit` green, no ceiling raised, no baseline re-recorded (**B1178** remains open).
- **WHAT IS LEFT, NAMED AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED HERE.** The largest remaining mover is the planner render body (+92.6 ms across 0 → 16 ponds): **`pondLedgerEntries` is built in the render body, per render, per pond** (`SitePlanner.jsx:10533–10566` — `ringOf` ×3, `incrementalExcavationCf`, `pondSplitFor` → `usablePondVolume` → `bandedStorage`, `detentionStorage`, `detWithAuto`), none of which takes the view, ~127 times per gesture. It is the B1352/B1437 class exactly. It is **not** fixed here for a rule reason, not a time one: the heavy geometry beneath is already memoised, so hoisting it means a `useMemo` over TWELVE inputs, and a hand-maintained dependency list that misses one is a **stale engineering ledger** — a wrong detention volume presented as current. Done properly it needs the B1352 treatment (a resolved record whose identity IS the evidence). Filed as **B221763**.

- **THE MISS, and the owner was right about it.** Every number this speed program has produced came from Goose Creek or a scene derived from it. He has reported TWO sites as slow — Bain and Sylvestri — and the harness could open neither. So the instrument has been measuring the one site it CAN open while he reports on two it cannot, and calling the result a floor. **`ui-audit/fixtures/bain-concept-a.json`** ends that: 53 elements in his exact measured kind counts (building 12 · sidewalk 12 · parking 12 · road 8 · paving 6 · trailer 2 · pond 1), 5 parcels, and **both rasters at their exact measured dimensions, opacities, `ftPerPx` and IndexedDB-string storage path** — 1728 × 2592 @ 0.55 over 1800 × 1167 @ 1.0. Settings/origin/county are held EQUAL to the Goose Creek control so the comparison isolates rasters instead of confounding them.
- **THE INSTRUMENT THE PROGRAM DID NOT HAVE, and its absence is why this could not have been found before.** Every cost metric here is `ScriptDuration + LayoutDuration + RecalcStyleDuration`. All three are main-thread work that happens BEFORE a pixel exists, so **none of them can see paint, raster, image decode or compositing** — which is exactly where a large translucent overlay spends its time. `ui-audit/lib/rasterCost.mjs` adds that half from Chromium's own tracing, bucketed by name and differenced across the same viewport-neutral pan.
- **THE STATISTICS, because the verdicts below depend on them and the obvious one does not work here.** Two independent batteries (4 reps + 6 reps, **60 runs, 0 suppressed**), arms INTERLEAVED. The repo's usual noise floor is a RANGE — `(max − min) / median` — which grows monotonically with n, so one contaminated rep set it (±48.4% at 4 reps) and no amount of extra data could ever tighten it. **The floor is reported unchanged and clears nothing**; what is ADDED is the analysis the interleaved design already supported and nobody was reading — a **paired sign test rep-for-rep**, which cancels a slow machine-minute because it hits both arms together. Bar declared in code ahead of any result (p ≤ 0.05); six paired reps is the arithmetic minimum it can speak at.
- **(a) SEMI-TRANSPARENCY IS NOT THE MECHANISM — the hypothesis named first is dead.** Forcing the overlay to opacity 1.0 (same pixels, same footprint, alpha removed) separates on **NOTHING**: paint 5/10, raster 6/10, composite 7/10, render 8/10 — not one bucket reaches p ≤ 0.05.
- **(b) NOR IS PIXEL COUNT. The cost tracks the AREA THE OVERLAY COVERS, not its resolution.** `quarter` cuts both rasters to ¼ the pixels **while holding the on-map footprint exactly** — decoded texture 17.1 → 4.3 MB, a 75% cut — and raster work falls **6.3%** (9/10, p=0.021). Removing the overlay outright falls **24.3%** (9/10, p=0.021). Three quarters of the texture buys a quarter of the saving.
- **(c) BECAUSE THE OVERLAY NEVER GETS ITS OWN COMPOSITOR LAYER — and this one count explains (a) and (b) together.** **304 layers with it · 304 at quarter size · 304 opaque · 304 hidden · 304 with both rasters gone.** Identical in every arm of every run. It is painted into the MAIN CONTENT LAYER, so it is re-rastered as part of that layer's tiles at SCREEN scale over the area it covers: alpha is free because the blend rides a raster pass that was going to run anyway, and source resolution is nearly free because the raster is at screen scale, not image scale.
- **(d) AND MOST OF BAIN'S COST IS NOT THE RASTERS AT ALL.** Bain's render work is **40% above** Goose Creek's (9/10, p=0.021). **Strip BOTH rasters out of Bain and it is still 20.9% above** (9/10, p=0.021), with **composite +55.6% and layerize +46.4%, both at 10/10 (p=0.002)**. Roughly half the gap is rasters and roughly half is Bain's own scene — 1,035 canvas nodes against 884, and **304 compositor layers against 118**. Nothing here explains where 304 layers come from; it is the largest deterministic difference between the two plans and the next thing to measure.
- **(e) MAIN-THREAD WORK IS IDENTICAL ON THE TWO PLANS — which is the whole story of the miss in one line.** Script + layout + style: **5 of 10 paired reps, p = 1.000.** Bain 795 ms, Goose Creek 790 ms. **The only cost metric this program owns cannot tell the two plans apart.** Every difference above lives in paint, raster, composite and layerize, and the un-quantised work figure is structurally blind to all four.
- **(f) THE FRAME MEDIAN IS BLIND TOO** — 50.0 ms on `bain`, 49.9 on `goose`, 50.0 on `quarter` and `no-rasters`, pinned to three display frames. The B1432 quantisation trap arriving in a new place.
- **(g) A PRODUCT FACT FOUND BY THE HARNESS REFUSING AN ARM IT COULD NOT PROVE.** The aerial UNDERLAY is **never painted** on any plan with an origin — `showAerial && underlay && !(origin && basemapOn)`, and `basemapSrc` initialises to `"esri"` whenever a plan has an origin with no persisted preference that could turn it off. "26 MB of decoded texture" was wrong: it is **17.1 MB painted**, plus one raster held in memory and never composited.
- **(h) THE 10 MB STRINGS ARE READ ONCE, NOT PER FRAME, and the heap agrees.** The load effect selects only overlays with `(idbKey || storageKey) && !src`, so once `src` is filled it never re-reads; it is then held in React state for the session. Measured settled heap: `bain` **67 MB** · `quarter` (same scene, quarter-size strings) **33 MB** · `goose` (no rasters) **26 MB**.
- **(i) AND THE OVERLAY DOES RIDE THE B1440 PAN ANCHOR.** It renders inside `<g transform={panT}>` and positions through `f2p`, which reads the anchored `renderView`, so during an armed pan its `x`/`y`/`width`/`height` do not change — one transform, not a re-registration per frame.
- **⚠ (j) ONE COST THIS FIXTURE DOES NOT REPRODUCE, and it is a LEAD rather than a result.** His real overlay is **page 1 of a PDF**, and B749 re-rasters a PDF-backed overlay at up to 8192 px once magnification exceeds ~1.5× its base raster — gated on `overlayDocs.has(id) || storageKey.endsWith(".pdf")`. The fixture's overlay is a bare image with no PDF source, so **that path never ran in any arm here.** It fires on ZOOM, not pan, and it is the obvious next suspect for "Bain gets slow when I zoom in."
- **⛔ THE GUARD THAT MAKES ALL OF THE ABOVE MEAN ANYTHING.** An arm whose raster never decoded looks *exactly* like an arm that is fast. The first run of this harness wrote NOTHING to IndexedDB — Playwright evaluates a STRING as an expression and does not call it with the argument, unlike Puppeteer — and every arm would have reported a beautiful null result. `decodeFault` refuses to report any arm until every expected raster has resolved `decode()` at intrinsic dimensions read from the element's OWN bytes (an `<image>` in SVG is an `SVGImageElement` and has no `naturalWidth`, so the obvious check does not exist).
- **⚠ AND ONE NUMBER WAS WRONG BEFORE IT WAS PUBLISHED.** Chromium's render events NEST — `ZeroCopyRasterBuffer::Playback` and `DisplayItemList::Raster` run inside a `RasterTask` — and summing the unrecognised names into the total double-counted the same microseconds, inflating every arm by ~60%. Fixed, unit-tested, and the battery re-run from scratch rather than corrected on paper.
- **What this still cannot settle, stated rather than implied.** Raster CONTENT is synthetic; the geometry is synthesised to his counts, not his coordinates; the sandbox blocks every external host so GIS and Supabase are ABSENT, not slow. Every figure is a LOWER BOUND, and the ~21-point geometry gap in particular is measured on invented coordinates.

Expect a `BACKLOG.md` conflict (main's copy moved); resolve by keeping both sides' items and **renumber nothing**. Then **wait out the ~30-minute lag before concluding anything** — a PR reading `Expected` for the first half hour is normal. That last sentence is the one that would have prevented six renumbers.

An **export pass now bypasses the anchor entirely** (`!exportPass && …`), i.e. the sheet resolves its own render view at export time instead of inheriting whatever transient state the screen is holding. A sheet built mid-gesture is identical to one built at rest **by construction**. This is the same principle B1355 already shipped under — *an export is a document, not a screenshot* — applied to the view rather than to a label gate.
